outline.description: This chapter introduces the statutory framework of the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) and the specific exemption at issue in this case—Exemption 7(A). It covers FOIA's general disclosure mandate, the role of statutory exemptions, the text and requirements of Exemption 7(A), the 'pending or reasonably anticipated' standard for enforcement proceedings, and the segregability requirement that obligates agencies to release nonexempt information. This provides the legal foundation necessary to understand the parties' arguments and the court's analysis.
subtopics: FOIA's general disclosure mandate under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(3)
The role of statutory exemptions under 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)
Text and elements of Exemption 7(A): records 'compiled for law enforcement purposes' whose disclosure 'could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings'
The 'pending or reasonably anticipated' standard for enforcement proceedings (CREW v. DOJ)
The segregability requirement under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) and § 552(b)

outline.description: This chapter traces the factual and procedural history of the case, from Farahi's personal background and immigration proceedings to the FBI's handling of his FOIA request and the ensuing litigation. It covers the initial summary judgment motion supported by Hardy declarations, the district court's concerns about staleness and segregability, the FBI's supplemental submissions with Bender declarations, the district court's grant of summary judgment, and Farahi's appeal. Understanding this procedural arc is essential to grasping why the court addressed staleness, ex parte submissions, and segregability as it did.

The Bender supplemental declarations and renewed summary judgment motion
The district court's grant of summary judgment and Farahi's appeal

outline.chapter_title: Standards of Review and Evidentiary Framework
outline.description: This chapter explains the legal standards governing the court's review of the FBI's withholding decisions. It covers the de novo standard for summary judgment in FOIA cases, the government's burden of proof, the deference owed to the FBI as a law enforcement agency—particularly in national security and counterterrorism matters—and the standards for each element of Exemption 7(A). It also addresses the standard for withholding records in their entirety when nonexempt portions are inextricably intertwined with exempt ones, and the court's reliance on agency affidavits.

The 'inextricably intertwined' standard for withholding records in full (Juarez, Mead Data Central)

outline.chapter_title: Application of Exemption 7(A) to Farahi's Records
outline.description: This chapter examines how the court applied the two elements of Exemption 7(A) to the withheld records. It analyzes the law enforcement purposes element, including the Hardy declaration's showing and Farahi's own concessions about his connections to terrorist organizations. It then addresses the interference element, including the government's evidentiary showings across multiple declarations, Farahi's staleness argument, the court's reasoning that the Bender declaration should be read as an update rather than in isolation, and the contextual significance of the investigation's breadth. It also covers Farahi's forfeited challenge to the FBI's document categorization.

outline.chapter_title: Segregability Analysis and Ex Parte Declarations
outline.description: This chapter addresses the final legal issues in the case: whether the FBI satisfied its obligation to segregate and release nonexempt information, and whether the district court improperly relied on ex parte declarations. It covers the statutory segregability requirement, the standard for when nonexempt material is not reasonably segregable, Farahi's argument that the volume of records necessarily implies segregable information, the court's distinction between individual words and meaningful information, and the role of ex parte declarations in FOIA litigation involving national security.
